how_to_read_the_warrant_field.the_three_warrants: INK, ORANGE, BLUE — in that order, which is the mark's order and the order they are named in everywhere else. They are KINDS of warrant, not levels of one: the argument a person refereed is not the weak version of the proof a machine checked.
how_to_read_the_warrant_field.ink: THE INK WARRANT. An argument written out for a human reader and refereed. The row pins it to a hashed document at a named location, so a reader can check they are reading the bytes the row cites; its ancestry was refereed at source, per row; and the proof itself was read by an independent adversarial referee, recorded at edition level. This is a warrant, not the absence of one — a refereed informal proof is what the other two are checked against. WHAT IT DOES NOT YET CARRY, stated because the other two warrants do carry it: a per-row record of WHO refereed THIS claim and when. Refereeing of the sources is per row; refereeing of the argument is recorded for the edition. Neither is yet a per-claim anchor.
how_to_read_the_warrant_field.orange: THE ORANGE WARRANT. Verified by computation over the bound in declared_range, and over nothing else. The bound is part of the claim.
how_to_read_the_warrant_field.blue: THE BLUE WARRANT. A Lean declaration states THIS ROW'S claim and its #print axioms result is exactly the clean triple with no sorryAx. The axioms field is the ACTUAL measured result, never a restatement of the sandbox's closed status.
how_to_read_the_warrant_field.the_rule_that_matters: warrant describes THIS ROW, not the sandbox. sandboxA0a is closed with a clean axiom triple; that does not make every row the blue warrant. A row whose Lean declaration is absent is not blue-warranted however completely the sandbox is certified.
how_to_read_the_warrant_field.and_the_one_that_matters_more: A row may not carry the blue warrant on the strength of a Lean proof if the claim the row makes is about the CODE. See EMBEDDING_NOTE.md §5. The Lean declaration certifies the Lean statement. Nothing else.

literature: Harman–Hopkins, Quantum integer-valued polynomials, arXiv:1601.06110, §1 (quantum Pólya basis) and §4 (bilateral localization)
rows.convention_frame: As row 01, PLUS the transport that makes the citation apply at all. Their grid is ADDITIVE (integrality imposed at the q-integers x = [n]_q); ours is MULTIPLICATIVE (Y̌ = q^m). The two are exchanged by the node-preserving substitution Y̌ = 1 + (q−1)x, which is invertible over Q(q) but not over Z[q^{±1}], so it does NOT map Z[q^{±1}][x] into Z[q^{±1}][Y̌]. Because integrality is imposed AT THE NODES and the nodes correspond, the substitution nevertheless carries their lattice ISOMORPHICALLY onto ours, taking each of their basis elements to nu_k(Y̌) term by term. (Corrected 2026-08-13: this edition previously denied it was a lattice isomorphism, which was false — the transport is legitimate precisely because it is one; what fails is only the naive map of coefficient lattices.) Their Gaussian binomial is ONE-SIDED (differs from the symmetric convention by a unit power of q: integrality survives, explicit coefficients do not). Their §1 works over Z[q], a PROPER subring of A_t; the bilateral statement needed here is §4, where the localization inverts q ONLY — not t, not cyclotomic factors. NAME COLLISION, and the migration made it worse: their z is our Y̌; our free parameter is t; today's letter z is the square root of t.

CARD: lit-cahen-chabert-vandermonde-coefficient-descent (Librarian, 2026-08-13, verified at source). CAHEN-CHABERT, Integer-Valued Polynomials, AMS Surveys 48, PROPOSITION I.3.1 with REMARKS I.3.2(i)-(ii), printed p. 9 (section I.3 'Trivial cases', subsection 'Vandermonde' — NOT section I.2 Localization, which is adjacent only). Prop I.3.1: for D a domain in a field L and f of degree n with coefficients in L, if f takes values in D at n+1 points a_0..a_n of D, then d*f is in D[X] where d = prod_{i<j}(a_j - a_i) is the Vandermonde. Remark I.3.2(i) draws exactly this row's claim: 'if E is an infinite subset of K, then a polynomial with coefficients in a LARGER FIELD which maps E into D is in fact a polynomial with coefficients in K. Hence there is no lack of generality in defining Int(E,D) as a subset of K[X].' Remark I.3.2(ii) names the enlarged-ambient object Int(E,D,L) and records that it is a genuinely NEW object only when E is FINITE. Ours is infinite. FRAME: their D is our A_t = Z[v^{±1},t^{±1}] (infinite domain); their K is Frac(A_t) = Q(v,t); their L is any larger field; their E is our multiplicative grid {q^chi : chi in Z}; their Int(E,D) is N^ev. Their hypotheses hold verbatim: the nodes q^chi lie IN the domain, not merely in its fraction field. WHY THE SHARP FORM MATTERS AND THE REMARK ALONE WOULD NOT: Remark I.3.2(i) lands the coefficients in the QUOTIENT FIELD, whereas this row needs them in F_t = Q(v)[t^{±1}], which is NOT a field. Prop I.3.1 is sharper than the remark drawn from it — it lands them in (1/d)*A_t with d an EXPLICIT product of node differences. Since every node is a power of q, that d lies in Z[q^{±1}] and carries NO t, so no t can enter a denominator: the non-field landing is exactly what the explicit Vandermonde gives. ADJACENT AND EXPLICITLY REJECTED (recorded so nobody re-searches them): all of section I.2 (localizes the target domain or the evaluation set, never the ambient); IV.3 Prop IV.3.4 / Cor IV.3.5 pp.82-84 (vary the evaluation SUBRING); section IV.4 (integral closure of Int(E,D), a different question); Ch IV Exercise 3 p.91 (E in F in K with F a subfield — again the evaluation set); and Harman-Hopkins section 4 Prop 4.3, rejected earlier and still rejected. Across the whole book exactly THREE passages vary a field at all, and only p.9 varies the ambient.
